The way I've always looked at it, the first few (for arguments sake) amendments can be summed up like this:

  1. You can say what you would like and when you would like, worship or not whomever you would like, and this extends to the press.
  2. You have the right to defend yourself.
  3. You cannot be forced to house soldiers.
  4. Your house/car/pockets are your property, you do not have to divulge what is in them without a warrant or when being arrested.
  5. You cannot be forced to say something that will incriminate yourself, hence the 1st amendment.

So taking these into context, we'll focus on the 2nd one. You have the right to defend yourself, as every human does. What happens if someone else comes to you with a tank and says, "Your house is mine now" but the government said you really only needed a pocket knife to defend yourself. Because that's reasonable. Not fair, is it?

Now, before I get downgoated into the 9th circle, I'll explain why I brought this hypothetical situation up. You have the right to defend yourself, and if you have no reasonable way to defend yourself, then your right has been denied. At least, that is my opinion. Does this mean everyone should have the ability to have a tank? Sure, I think that is fine. Until an individual does something that is against the law, they should be presumed innocent in all ways. I feel this is an important thing to hold to, because if we don't assume innocence first we'll see shadows and jump at them. We'll believe someone has evil intent, and therefore they are already condemned and should be punished. Even though they haven't even done anything.

On to the psychology assessment. Considering recent news that just under two-thirds of psychological experiments that showed a statistically significant result set couldn't be reliably reproduced. The experiments were more recent ones that were published in three major publications. Nearly half of them couldn't reproduce the results at all, the remainder of reproduced results making up the "just under two-thirds" could get a similar set of results but had a diminished statistical margins. This, I think, is a serious concern when it comes to being able to effectively profile someone. It would be unreasonable to require someone to undergo the extensive and both time and monetarily expensive process of getting reliable results. Because there is no reasonable way to do it without a great cost and burden, I don't think it would do any good at all. Adding them would, arguably, make the ability to own a gun become unreasonable and thus a right inhibited at the best and denied at the worst.

TL;DR: Adding a psychology evaluation to the process of getting a gun costs too much, doesn't work as well as you might think, and overall would just suck for everyone.
